passage: Nine-year-old Wasim sat on the back step with an empty water bowl in his lap. Biscuit, his dog, had died in the night, and the crying would not stop. His father, Jeevan, sat down beside him and wrapped an arm around his shoulders. "It's okay to cry," Jeevan said. "I'm sad too." Wasim felt a little less alone. Later, in a low voice, he told his aunt Keerthana, "Biscuit didn't finish his dinner on Sunday and I didn't tell anyone. If I'd noticed, maybe he'd still be here." Keerthana put down the vegetables. "Wasim, lots of children think they should have saved a pet. But you walked him, washed him and gave him your biscuits every single day. That's how much you loved him." That evening Wasim found a shoebox and filled it with the red collar, a photo and the tennis ball. He wrote BISCUIT on the lid, and Jeevan helped him choose a shelf where it could stay.

qa.q: What did Wasim put in the shoebox?
qa.a: He put in the red collar, a photo and the tennis ball.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's response to Wasim's crying differ from Keerthana's response to his guilty thought?
qa.a: Jeevan sat beside him and said it was okay to cry, which made Wasim feel less alone, while Keerthana answered his guilt by reminding him how he walked, washed and gave his biscuits to Biscuit every day.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he told Keerthana about the dinner, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt guilty; he spoke in a low voice and wondered if noticing sooner would have kept Biscuit here.

qa.q: What could Wasim and Jeevan do with the shoebox in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: They could look at it together and share stories about Biscuit whenever Wasim feels sad.

grounding: A child mourning a dog is comforted by his father's hug, carries a guilty thought that an adult gently lifts, and finds a way to say goodbye.

passage: The bank-exam form sat on the dining table like a bill. Himani knew her father, Jatin, had worn the same watch for eleven years so her fees could be paid, and the thought sat heavy on her chest. "Your cousin Francis just got his first salary," her mother said, buttering toast. "Forty thousand." Himani set her cup down. "Ma, when you say that, I hear that I'm not enough. It hurts." Her mother blinked and went quiet. Himani did not spend the evening resenting Francis; she texted him congratulations. Later she sat with her father. "Papa, why do you want the bank job for me? I'd like to hear it before I decide. I'm thinking of design, and we may not agree." Jatin talked about the year his shop closed and the fear that followed. She listened, then said, "I'll prepare for the exam and I'll apply to the studio. Either way, the decision is mine." Walking home, she realised the man who always seemed certain had been frightened all along, and had sometimes snapped at her mother for no reason. She felt a small sadness for the father in her head, and a new warmth for the one who lived with them.

qa.q: Whose first salary did Himani's mother mention?
qa.a: She mentioned her cousin Francis's first salary.

qa.q: How did Himani's reaction to the comparison with Francis differ from how she spoke with her father about the bank job?
qa.a: With her mother she said the comparison hurt and then congratulated Francis instead of resenting him; with her father she asked for his reasons, disagreed politely, and said the decision was hers.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as she thought about her father's watch?
qa.a: She felt grateful and burdened at once, because the thought sat heavy on her chest.

qa.q: What could Himani do to honour her parents' effort while keeping her choice?
qa.a: She could prepare for the exam and apply to the studio, keep listening to her father's reasons, and make the final decision herself.

grounding: A young adult's love for her parents, hurt at a comparison, polite disagreement and a new view of her father as an imperfect person unfold in one household.

passage: When the coach read out the new debate captain, it was Gopika's name. Zeenat's stomach clenched. She had wanted that badge for two years. That night she admitted the envy to herself, then watched a recording of Gopika's last round and wrote down how she opened with a story and paused before every rebuttal. At the next practice Zeenat asked her for tips, and they argued the same motion from opposite sides, grinning whenever a point landed. Nazia stood by the door. "You only got it because the coach likes you," she told Gopika. Gopika went hot, because a small voice in her had wondered the same. She did not snap back. After practice she asked the coach for honest feedback on her speeches and left with three things to work on. Nazia could not bear even hearing Gopika's name, and her jaw tightened whenever it came up in the team chat. She realised she had thought about nothing else all week, and her own speech on water saving was still half-written. She closed the chat and opened her notebook. 🙂

qa.q: What did Zeenat write down after watching Gopika's recording?
qa.a: She wrote down that Gopika opened with a story and paused before every rebuttal.

qa.q: How did Zeenat's response to Gopika winning differ from Nazia's?
qa.a: Zeenat admitted her envy, studied Gopika's round and became friendly, while Nazia could not bear Gopika's name and sneered at her; only later did she turn back to her own speech.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when Nazia said the coach liked her, and why did it sting?
qa.a: She felt hot with hurt, because a small voice in her had wondered the same thing.

qa.q: What could Nazia do to stop her feelings from draining her energy?
qa.a: She could keep her attention on her own speech and goals, as she did when she opened her notebook, rather than on Gopika.

grounding: After one debate captaincy, one rival admires and learns, another sneers, the winner takes the sneer to a mentor, and a hater redirects her energy.

passage: In the office pantry, a senior colleague mimicked Jatin's accent and joked that people from his region never finish anything on time. Others chuckled. Shreya laughed weakly too, then said nothing. Jatin's face went hot. He set down his cup and left. All afternoon Shreya's chest felt tight. That evening she messaged him: "I should have said something. Are you okay?" Jatin wrote back that a landlord had turned him away that same week; the man had looked at his surname and said the flat was taken. Jatin felt angry and small, though he knew it said more about the landlord than about him. Shreya helped him list other flats, and they wrote down the dates of both incidents. The next morning, when the same colleague made another joke, Shreya said evenly, "That's not funny." Jatin later took his notes to a senior in HR. Devika, who had watched all this, had caught herself that week assuming the new hire from the north would be rude. She noticed the thought without punishing herself, sat beside him at lunch, and found him funnier and kinder than her guess.

qa.q: What did Shreya message Jatin that evening?
qa.a: She wrote that she should have said something and asked if he was okay.

qa.q: How did Shreya's second reaction to the colleague's jokes differ from her first, and what had changed?
qa.a: The first time she laughed weakly and said nothing; the next morning she said evenly, "That's not funny," after feeling tight-chested all afternoon and checking on Jatin.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when the landlord said the flat was taken, and what did he understand about it?
qa.a: He felt angry and small, though he knew the refusal said more about the landlord than about him.

qa.q: What could Devika keep doing to test her own assumptions about people?
qa.a: She could keep sitting with people, as she did at lunch, and compare her guesses with what they are actually like.

grounding: Colleagues and a landlord treat Jatin with prejudice, while a bystander moves from silence to support and another notices her own assumption.

passage: Before the bell, Karthik leaned over Baljeet's desk. "Lend me your maths homework. Real friends let each other copy, you know." Baljeet's stomach flipped; he did want to help. "I am your friend," he said. "That's why I'll show you how to do the first sum, and then you try the rest." Karthik grumbled, but at recess they sat together and got three sums done. In art class Shreya groaned, having forgotten her colours. Baljeet slid his box across the desk without a second thought. By afternoon the box had not come back, so he asked, "Could I have my colours, please? I need the blue." She apologised and returned them at once. At lunch Ritesh sat beside him, chatty and full of jokes, and shared half a mango. Ten minutes later he asked to borrow Baljeet's new pen, then his eraser. Baljeet realised Ritesh had not spoken to him all week. "Sorry, I need them today," he said, and left it at that.

qa.q: What did Baljeet lend Shreya in art class?
qa.a: He lent her his box of colours.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's answer to Karthik differ from his reaction when Shreya needed colours, and why?
qa.a: He would not hand over his homework and offered to show Karthik the first sum so he could learn, but he freely lent Shreya his colours, a small loan, and politely asked for them back when they were late.

qa.q: What was Baljeet likely feeling when Ritesh asked for the pen and then the eraser?
qa.a: He probably felt used, because Ritesh had not spoken to him all week and was friendly only when he wanted something.

qa.q: What could Baljeet say next time a friend uses guilt to ask for answers?
qa.a: He could say he is their friend and will teach them, then offer to sit together and work it out. 🙂

grounding: Four requests from classmates show pressure, help with limits, easy generosity and being used by someone who is friendly only when they need something.

passage: The class group chat lit up at nine. Chaitanya had written, "Kiran's talk was so dull I nearly slept." Kiran's ears burned, and his thumbs hovered over a reply that would humiliate Chaitanya in front of forty people. He put the phone down, drank some water, then opened a private chat. "That comment stung. Can we talk?" A minute later came: "Sorry. It was a stupid joke." The next day a rumour appeared: Vinita had copied her science project. Her first instinct was to delete the app and vanish. Instead she told her mother and the class teacher, then wrote one message in the group with her draft and its dates attached, and let it stand. Two friends sat with her at lunch. That evening someone shared a voice note of a shy boy, Ravi, stumbling over a poem, and the chat filled with laughing faces. Chaitanya typed a mocking line too, because he did not want to be the next target. The moment he sent it, his stomach dropped. He deleted it, but people had already seen it, so he messaged Ravi: "That was unkind of me. I liked your poem." 🙂

qa.q: How many people were in the class group chat?
qa.a: Forty people were there.

qa.q: How did Kiran's way of handling Chaitanya's harsh comment differ from Chaitanya's behaviour toward Ravi's voice note?
qa.a: Kiran put the phone down and took his hurt to a private chat, while Chaitanya joined the public mocking for fear of being next and only afterwards sent Ravi a private apology.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when the rumour appeared, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: She felt afraid enough to want to vanish, but she told her mother and the class teacher and corrected the rumour once with her draft.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya do next time the chat starts mocking someone?
qa.a: He could stay out of it or send the person a kind private message straight away, before anyone else joins in.

grounding: One class group chat holds a rumour, a friend's harsh comment answered privately, and a boy who joins mockery out of fear then makes amends.
